What you get in this pack
Five complete Teacher Packs, one for each level, so you can teach any learner from age 4 upwards
and move them on when they are ready.
5 Teacher
Packs,
Levels
1–5
Each is a licensed PDF with the syllabus, the manual and forty lesson plans, with a contents page.

pages
in

Lesson 11: Excavation — Discovering Feeling Fossils in Owl
Babies
Target
Grade
Level
/
Subject
/
Duration
Grade
Level: Ages 4–8 (CEFR Pre-A1 →  A1)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 1: Foundation)
Duration: 40 minutes
Overall
Learning
Goals
Students will transition into a regulated state of physiological readiness (the "Green Zone") to actively listen to a
weighty literary text about separation and wait time. They will excavate "Word Fossils" from the narrative —
vocabulary that captures the somatic experience of anxiety and the relief of return.
Speciﬁc
Learning
Objectives
1. Students will independently or semi-independently execute the "Butterﬂy Hug" self-regulation protocol to
achieve physiological readiness.
2. Students will identify and extract at least one speciﬁc "Word Fossil" (e.g., worried,
scared,
dark,
alone,
brave) from the read-aloud text.
3. Students will accurately connect their identiﬁed "Word Fossil" to a corresponding visual representation
(Emotion Icon or book illustration of Sarah, Percy, or Bill).
Materials
Needed
Core Text: Owl
Babies by Martin Waddell (physical book and/or audio-visual representation).
Emotion
Icons: Laminated cards featuring clear facial expressions or physical states (worried, scared,
alone, brave, relieved/happy).
Word
Wall
Materials: Blank cards, thick markers, and designated wall space.
Fidget
Fossils: Small, smooth stones provided for students requiring tactile neurodiverse accommodations.
Nature
Anchor: A visible natural object in the classroom — for this text, ideally a small branch or piece of
bark to evoke the owls' tree.

Detailed
Procedure
/
Step-by-Step
Outline
Phase
1:
Regulation-Before-Reasoning
(0–5
minutes)
Activity: The Butterﬂy Hug Protocol.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Paleontologists,
today
we
are
visiting
a
dark
forest
where
three
baby
owls
are
waiting.
Before
we
can
sit
with
them
in
the
dark,
we
must
get
our
brains
and
bodies
into
the
Green
Zone.
Cross
your
arms,
hook
your
thumbs,
and
tap
left,
right,
left,
right.
Breathe
quietly
with
me
for
60
seconds."
Student
Task: Students perform the Butterﬂy Hug, focusing on bilateral tapping and silent breathing to
regulate their autonomic nervous systems.
Action: Distribute "Fidget Fossils" to ADHD-proﬁle and high-anxiety students. Note: the Owl
Babies text is
emotionally activating for some children with separation anxiety — anchor objects are essential.
Phase
2:
The
Dig
Site
—
Active
Reading
(5–15
minutes)
Activity: Read-aloud of Owl
Babies.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Today,
we
are
looking
for
Word
Fossils
—
words
that
tell
us
how
the
three
baby
owls
feel
inside
their
bodies
while
they
wait
for
their
mother.
Listen
to
Sarah,
Percy,
and
little
Bill.
When
you
hear
a
feeling,
touch
your
nose."
Student
Task: Active listening. Students use the tactile gesture (touching nose) when identifying a target
word.
Action: Read the text slowly. Emphasize target BICS/CALP crossover vocabulary: worried,
scared,
dark,
alone,
brave,
soft. Pay particular attention to the smallest owl's repeated cry for his mother as the somatic
anchor for anxiety. Do not stop for grammar instruction.
Phase
3:
Excavation
—
The
Word
Fossil
Hunt
(15–30
minutes)
Activity: Identifying and claiming vocabulary.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Paleontologists,
what
Word
Fossils
did
we
ﬁnd
in
the
dark
layers
of
this
story?
What
words
tell
us
how
the
owls
felt
while
they
waited?"
Student
Task: Students verbally share a feeling word they noticed in the text.
Teacher
Move
(Marking): When a student says "Worried" or "Scared," the teacher executes the
Accountable Talk "Marking" move: "You
found
a
fossil.
'Worried'
is
what
your
tummy
feels
when
you
don't
know
if
someone
is
coming
back.
Let's
put
that
on
our
Word
Wall." Write the word clearly on a card and
place it on the board.
Action: Continue until 3–4 key feeling words are "excavated" and placed on the Word Wall. Aim for at least
one Tier 2 fossil (e.g., worried or brave) beyond the basic sad/happy.
Phase
4:
Linguistic
Connection
&
UDL
Expression
(30–35
minutes)
Activity: Connecting text to visual evidence (A1 Indicator prep).
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "I
am
holding
up
a
picture
of
little
Bill
on
the
branch,
calling
out
for
his
mother.
Which
Word
Fossil
from
our
wall
matches
Bill's
face
and
body?"
Student
Task: Students point to or verbally identify the correct Word Fossil (e.g., "Worried" or "Scared")
that matches the provided Emotion Icon or book illustration.

Lesson 13: Excavation — Explicit Evidence and Causality in
The Iron Man
Target
Grade
Level
/
Subject
/
Duration
Grade
Level: Ages 8–10 (CEFR A1 →  A2)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 2: Development)
Duration: 45 minutes
Overall
Learning
Goals
Students will open the Iron
Man dig site by distinguishing explicit text from inference. Ted Hughes's opening —
the Iron Man at the cliﬀ edge, the fall, the reassembly — is one of the most evocative passages in 20th-century
children's literature. Today's job: separate what the text actually
says from what the reader imagines and fears.
Speciﬁc
Learning
Objectives
1. Students will independently initiate the Butterﬂy Hug or Cool Down Pass.
2. Students will distinguish explicit textual statements from inferred meaning in Chapter 1 of The
Iron
Man.
3. Students will locate, highlight (blue), and cite (page + paragraph) at least three pieces of explicit evidence
about the Iron Man's appearance and arrival.
4. Students will pass the Parrot Eﬀect Check by orally interpreting cited evidence in their own words.
Materials
Needed
Core Text: The
Iron
Man by Ted Hughes (physical copies for all students).
Audio version queued for Chapter 1 (the cliﬀ fall and the reassembly).
Dual-coding
highlighters (Yellow / Blue).
Cool
Down
Passes at the front desk.
Accountable
Talk
Cards on student desks.
An "Explicit
vs.
Inferred"
T-chart projected or posted.
Detailed
Procedure
/
Step-by-Step
Outline
Phase
1:
Regulation
Transfer
(0–7
minutes)
Activity: Self-initiated regulation. Frame the new text.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "New
dig
site
today.
The
Iron
Man
is
a
story
about
something
most
people
are
afraid
of
—
a
giant
they
cannot
understand.
Some
of
you
may
feel
a
ﬂicker
of
that
fear
yourself
when
we
read.
That
is
normal.
Regulate
now.
Cool
Down
Passes
are
at
the
front."
Action: Brief Butterﬂy Hug. Conﬁrm Passes accessible.

Phase
2:
The
Dig
Site
—
Reading
for
the
Cliﬀ
Edge
(7–22
minutes)
Activity: Audio + text reading of Chapter 1.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Today
we
are
looking
for
explicit
evidence
ONLY.
We
are
not
looking
for
what
we
think
happened.
We
are
looking
for
what
Ted
Hughes
ACTUALLY
wrote.
Listen.
Follow
the
text.
Underline
nothing
yet."
Student
Task: Students follow physical text while audio plays through the Iron Man's appearance, the fall,
and the reassembly.
Action: Stop after the seagulls ﬂy past the reassembled Iron Man and he walks into the sea.
Phase
3:
Excavation
—
Locating
Explicit
Evidence
(22–37
minutes)
Activity: Dual-coding and citation hunt.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "I
have
three
Claims.
Prove
each
one
with
blue
evidence.
Citation
required:
page
and
paragraph.
Claim
1
—
'The
Iron
Man
is
enormous.'
Claim
2
—
'The
Iron
Man
fell
apart
at
the
bottom
of
the
cliﬀ.'
Claim
3
—
'The
Iron
Man
put
himself
back
together.'
Find
the
explicit
sentences.
Show
me
the
page."
Student
Task: Students scan, highlight in blue, and write the page/paragraph next to each highlighted
sentence.
Teacher
Move: Press relentlessly: "That's
not
the
page.
Show
me
the
paragraph.
Read
the
SENTENCE
that
proves
my
Claim.
Don't
summarize."
Explicit
vs.
Inferred
check: "Does
the
text
say
'the
Iron
Man
was
alive'?
Or
does
it
say
something
that
we
INFER
means
alive?
Look
carefully.
The
author's
exact
words
matter."
Phase
4:
The
Parrot
Eﬀect
Check
(37–43
minutes)
Activity: Verbal interpretation without the text in front.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Cover
the
book
with
your
hand.
In
your
own
words:
how
did
the
Iron
Man
put
himself
back
together?
What
did
the
text
actually
describe?"
Student
Task: Students orally interpret the reassembly without peeking.
Teacher
Move: "You
said
'magic.'
Did
the
text
use
the
word
'magic'?
Or
did
the
text
describe
each
piece
ﬁnding
the
next
piece?
That
is
the
diﬀerence
between
explicit
and
inferred."
Diﬀerentiation
/
Accommodations
Neuroinclusive
(Dyslexia): Audio runs the entire Phase 2. During Phase 3, pair the student with a peer who
reads the target paragraph aloud while the dyslexic student locates the highlight. Pre-chunked text version
available.
Neuroinclusive
(ADHD): Use Phase 3 as a movement break — student walks to a posted version of the
chapter on the wall and highlights there. Chunk the three Claims into one at a time.
Neuroinclusive
(Anxiety): Strict No Cold Call. Whisper-prompt the page in advance. Allow the student to
write the citation on a Post-it instead of speaking it.
Assessment
&
Rubric
Assessment
Type:
Formative
Observational
Assessment

Lesson 13: Excavation — Subtextual Observation and the
Threshold of Imagination in Bridge to Terabithia
Target
Grade
Level
/
Subject
/
Duration
Grade
Level: Ages 10–12 (CEFR A2 →  B1)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 3: Expansion)
Duration: 45 minutes
Overall
Learning
Goals
Students will open the Bridge
to
Terabithia dig site by separating Katherine Paterson's explicit text from the
dense subtext beneath it. The novel works almost entirely through implication — what Jess feels is rarely
named, but always traceable through what he does. Today: train the eye for B1-level subtextual observation.
Teacher
Pre-Note:
This
text
moves
toward
a
death
by
drowning.
Today's
lesson
opens
before
that
event.
Frame
the
text
honestly
—
students
should
know,
in
general
terms,
that
loss
is
part
of
the
story.
The
Cool
Down
Pass
and
Regulation
Station
are
essential
throughout
this
cycle.
Co-teach
with
a
counselor
available
if
possible.
The
manual
is
clear:
"Do
not
rescue
them
from
the
friction."
That
includes
grief
friction
—
but
it
does
NOT
mean
ignoring
it.
It
means
scaﬀolding
it,
holding
the
standard,
and
trusting
students
to
do
the
work.
Speciﬁc
Learning
Objectives
1. Students will independently regulate and locate the Cool Down Pass.
2. Students will distinguish explicit text from inferential subtext in the opening chapters.
3. Students will locate, dual-code (yellow=explicit, blue=inferred), and cite at least three pieces of evidence —
at least one of which requires inference to understand.
4. Students will articulate the diﬀerence between "what the text states" and "what the author implies" using B1
markers.
Materials
Needed
Core Text: Bridge
to
Terabithia by Katherine Paterson.
Audio version queued for the opening chapters.
Dual-coding
highlighters (Yellow=explicit; Blue=inferred).
Cool
Down
Passes.
Accountable
Talk
Reference
Cards.
B1
Interpretive
Marker
Poster.
Regulation
Station at the back of the room with a quiet light and Fidget Fossils.
"Explicit
vs.
Subtext"
T-chart projected.

Procedure
/
Step-by-Step
Outline
Phase
1:
Regulation
&
Framing
(0–8
minutes)
Activity: Self-regulation; honest framing of the text.

Scripting
Prompt: "This
dig
site
is Bridge to Terabithia.

book
is

about
loss.

minutes.

Cool

—
no

—

90
seconds

Phase
2:
The
Dig
Site
—
Reading
the
Opening
(8–22
minutes)
Activity: Audio + text reading of opening chapters.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Looking
for
two
things
today.
EXPLICIT
—
what
Paterson
actually
writes.
INFERRED
—
what
we
understand
without
her
writing
it.
She
rarely
tells
you

feels.
She
tells

what

The
feeling
is

Task: Follow audio with physical text.

Phase
3:
Excavation
—
Subtextual
Citation
(22–37
minutes)
Activity: Dual-coding the explicit/inferred distinction.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Three
Claims.
Citations
required.
Yellow
for
explicit;
Blue
for
inferred.
Claim
1
—
'Jess
practices
running
every
morning.'
That
should
be
EXPLICIT.
Claim
2
—
'Jess
is
angry
that
Leslie
won.'
That
is
INFERRED
—
Paterson
never
says
'angry.'
What
did
she
write
that
proves
it?
Claim
3
—
'Jess
and
his
father
do
not
understand
each
other.'
INFERRED.
What
evidence
proves
that
without
Paterson
stating
it
directly?"
Student
Task: Highlight in yellow OR blue depending on whether the citation is explicit or inferred. Cite
page/paragraph.
Teacher
Move: "You
highlighted
that
in
yellow.
Look
again.
Did
Paterson
actually
USE
the
word
'angry'?
No?
Then
it's
blue.
The
author
IMPLIES
anger.
That
is
subtext."
Phase
4:
B1
Marker
Practice
(37–43
minutes)
Activity: Verbal articulation of the explicit/subtext diﬀerence.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "For your blue highlights, complete this sentence aloud to your shoulder
partner: 'The author implies ___ because she writes ___.' Or: 'This evidence suggests ___ because the
underlying assumption is ___.' Use the markers."
Student
Task: Pair practice using B1 markers.
Teacher
Move: "Did
you
say
'the
text
says
Jess
is
angry'?
No,
the
text
doesn't
say
that.
Try:
'The
author
implies

angry
because
she

him
kicking
the
dirt.'
That's
B1."

(Executive

on the wall and highlights physically. One Claim at a time.

Lesson 13: Excavation — Visual Rhetoric and Linguistic
Deconstruction in Persepolis
Target
Grade
Level
/
Subject
/
Duration
Grade
Level: Ages 12–14 years
CEFR
Level: B1 →  B2 (Conquering the B2 Plateau)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 4: Mastery)
Duration: 45 minutes
Overall
Learning
Goals
Students open the Persepolis dig site and expand the Excavation toolkit. Marjane Satrapi's graphic memoir
delivers argument through TWO simultaneous channels — words AND images. Today: deconstruct how the
panel composition, the high-contrast black-and-white inking, and the child-narrator's voice operate together as
a rhetorical mechanism. The text demands the reader analyze what the picture says that the caption cannot.
Teacher
Pre-Note:
This
is
the
ﬁrst
text
in
the
JE
library
that
uses
visual
rhetoric
as
a
primary
argumentation
channel.
Anchor
the
historical
context
BEFORE
opening
the
panel:
the
Iranian
Revolution
of
1979,
the
Shah's
fall,
the
establishment
of
the
Islamic
Republic,
the
mandatory
veil,
the
Iran-Iraq
War.
The
manual
is
explicit:
"Do
not
teach
the
text
without
its
historical/political
anchor."
Speciﬁc
Learning
Objectives
1. Students will independently regulate.
